questions.evidence:
A media class watches a silent ten-second clip of a boy waiting beside a door. Before showing it, the teacher tells half the class that the boy is waiting for an exam result. The other half hears that he is waiting for a surprise birthday guest.

The first group often describes him as nervous. The second often calls him excited. Both groups saw the same clip, and the actor had been asked only to stand and look toward the door. The stories supplied beforehand shaped many interpretations.

Some students in each group choose different words, so the teacher avoids saying that background information controls every viewer. The class compares reports and marks which details were visible and which came from the introduction.

For their next film review, students plan to describe gestures before naming emotions. They can still make an interpretation, but they should explain its basis and consider alternatives. The activity shows how a small piece of surrounding information can change the story a viewer builds from an unchanged image.
